source.title: Understanding the Generalization of Adam in Learning Neural Networks with Proper Regularization
source.authors: Difan Zou; Yuan Cao; Yuanzhi Li; Quanquan Gu

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some equations and symbols are garbled by text extraction.
record.tranche_reason: Tests the Adam–GD generalization gap with weight decay in a theoretical synthetic-data setting and a reported AlexNet experiment, extending optimizer comparisons to these settings.
record.gate_note: The AlexNet figure reports noisier learned filters for Adam but no test-error result; recorded under fits_no_version. Cited findings from other studies are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares Adam and GD training and test errors in a new setting: two-layer CNNs on an image-inspired synthetic distribution. These results bear on V4's optimizer generalization comparison, although they do not reproduce its benchmark or tuning conditions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors attribute the synthetic CNN generalization gap to different feature-learning trajectories in a nonconvex objective, despite weight decay and identical initialization. They contrast this with successful optimization of convex objectives with quadratic regularization, where solutions coincide. These are setting-specific theoretical conclusions, not a demonstration that all regularization or tuning fails to improve Adam.
record.recipe_differences: The paper gives a theoretical analysis of full-batch Adam and GD on an image-inspired synthetic distribution, and a small numerical experiment; it does not reproduce the benchmark recipes in V4.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported optimizer gap depends on the objective setting: it appears for the nonconvex two-layer CNN synthetic-data setup and disappears in the convex setting with positive weight decay.

fits_no_version.finding: Under the convex theorem's assumptions, Adam and GD have test errors differing by at most o(1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For successfully optimized convex objectives with positive quadratic regularization, optimizer choice does not produce a persistent generalization difference.

fits_no_version.finding: Adam-trained AlexNet first-layer filters appear noisier than SGD-trained filters on CIFAR-10, without reported test errors.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer choice affects the qualitative appearance of learned first-layer filters under the reported AlexNet recipe.

record.problems: The main quantitative experiment uses a synthetic data distribution, one stated network width and one set of training hyperparameters; no uncertainty estimates are reported. The AlexNet result is qualitative and does not report test error.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its comparison with natural-label held-out accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.

Image and language benchmark performance under a specified limited tuning protocol; frequency across workloads; broader tuning; decoupled weight decay; switching optimizers; word-level language models. The synthetic experiment reports one recipe without a tuning search.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects and interactions with training-set size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps.
Removing highly memorized examples versus random examples and retraining.

missing.what: The central nonconvex theorem is missing: with probability at least 1 − 1/n, both optimizers attain zero training error, while Adam's population test error is at least 1/2 − o(1) and GD's is o(1). Record the distribution, width, step-size, iteration, and regularization assumptions. This independently supports V4's gap direction in the theoretical setting.
missing.locator: Theorem 4.1, Section 4; supporting Lemmas A.7 and A.14

record.verdict_notes: The convex equality result supplies no challenge to V4's qualified claim that adaptive methods often generalize worse on neural benchmarks. Theorem 4.1 gives a lower bound on Adam's test error, not equality to one-half. No uncertainty across experimental runs is reported.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or natural-label held-out comparison.
No width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected architectures.
Does not test image-classification or language benchmarks under limited hyperparameter tuning, broader tuning, decoupled weight decay, switching optimizers, or word-level language models.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare generalization measures.
Does not remove or retrain on memorized examples.

rows.subject: convex model with parameter W
rows.operation_detail: Theorem compares Adam and GD on a convex, smooth training objective with positive weight decay regularization.
rows.value: Both training errors are zero; test errors are equal up to ± o(1).
rows.note: The theorem states that Adam and GD reach the same solution when training is successful.
rows.check: The convex-objective theorem does not test V4's neural-network benchmark comparison under limited tuning. Its equality result should not receive a V4 scope verdict. Appendix B also conditions zero training error on sufficient overparameterization and feasibly small regularization; positive weight decay alone is insufficient.
